analysis.one_liner: Extends overtime, paid sick days, written contracts, and scheduling protections to domestic workers.
analysis.headline: The Domestic Workers Bill of Rights Act, cosponsored by 115 House Democrats, was introduced June 12, 2025, referred to six House committees, and has not advanced since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give the roughly 2.2 million people who clean homes, care for children, and aide seniors and people with disabilities in private homes the basic workplace rights most employees already have: overtime pay for live-in workers, up to seven paid sick days a year, written contracts, notice before schedule changes, meal and rest breaks, and protection from retaliation, including immigration threats. It would also ban wage deductions for breakage, add domestic workers to federal anti-discrimination law, and use a temporary Medicaid payment increase and grants to help fund compliance. The bill has sat in committee since introduction, with no hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic workers — nannies, housekeepers, home health and personal care aides, cooks, and caregivers — about 2.2 million people who are nearly 9 in 10 women, disproportionately people of color and immigrants, earning on average about $16.79 an hour. Live-in workers, who are currently excluded from federal overtime, would gain overtime, termination notice, severance or lodging, and guaranteed access to phone and internet. All covered workers would gain written agreements, paid sick time, schedule-change notice and reporting pay, breaks, privacy from employer monitoring, protection from immigration-related retaliation, and a right to sue. Families relying on in-home care would also benefit from lower turnover and more stable caregivers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Domestic workers, mostly women of color and immigrants

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal overtime exemption for live-in domestic workers, so employees who live in their employer's home would earn time-and-a-half beyond 40 hours a week.
Requires paid sick time of 1 hour per 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for a worker's own illness, a family member's care, or domestic violence and sexual assault-related needs.
Requires written contracts covering pay, hours, breaks, and termination policies, and bans forced arbitration, noncompete, and nondisclosure terms in those contracts.
Gives live-in workers fired without cause 30 days of lodging or two weeks' severance pay, plus written termination notice and guaranteed access to phone and internet.
Requires 72 hours' notice before schedule changes, pay for canceled or shortened shifts, and meal and rest breaks, with exceptions for emergencies and disability-related situations.

Bars employers from retaliating against workers who assert their rights, and treats immigration-related threats, including calling immigration authorities or filing false police reports, as prohibited discrimination.

Covers domestic workers under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, closing a gap that leaves most of them outside federal workplace anti-discrimination protections, and creates a national hotline, outreach grants, and a Domestic Employee Standards Board.

Temporarily raises the federal Medicaid match for home care delivered by domestic employees and delays enforcement for government-funded programs, so care recipients and states are not hit with disruption up front.

analysis.who_pays: Household employers — most directly families that hire nannies, housekeepers, or aides — would pay more in wages, overtime, sick time, scheduling pay, and paperwork, with compliance costs falling hardest on families hiring directly rather than through agencies. Home care and staffing agencies would face the same standards for their workforce. The temporary federal Medicaid match increase and the grants, hotline, and task force would be paid by the federal Treasury, and by state Medicaid programs to the extent the match increase ends. On-demand cleaning and care platforms could no longer shift communication costs onto workers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Household employers, home care agencies, and Medicaid

drawbacks.text: The costs land partly on ordinary households: a family hiring a part-time nanny or aide would owe written contracts, paid sick time, 72-hour schedule-change notice and reporting pay, and overtime for live-in workers, which could lead some middle-income families to reduce hours or hire less often.

The bill raises federal spending: it authorizes appropriations for grants, a hotline, a standards board, and an interagency task force, and temporarily increases the federal Medicaid match, adding to the deficit while it lasts.

Even with exceptions for medical emergencies, disasters, and disability-related cancellations, scheduling and break rules are harder for one-on-one care situations where the care recipient's needs cannot be paused, which is why the bill itself carves out shared living arrangements and delays enforcement for government-funded programs.

Enforcement relies on the Labor Department and private lawsuits; workers in isolated home settings with high fear of retaliation — the bill's own findings cite 91 percent of workers not complaining about conditions — may still not see these rights realized in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete for a workforce the bill's findings show earns about $16.79 an hour, works without contracts, and is largely excluded from overtime and federal anti-discrimination law. The honest costs are real: higher labor costs and paperwork for household employers, including middle-income families, and new federal spending, and the bill's own carve-outs — shared living arrangements, disability-related exceptions, delayed enforcement for government-funded care — show its authors recognized that rigid rules can clash with the unpredictable nature of home-based care. On balance, the bill transfers bargaining power in a deeply lopsided labor market to workers, and the design mitigations temper but do not eliminate the cost to families and Medicaid.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and sent to six House committees at once, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote since June 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Domestic Workers Bill of Rights Act on June 12, 2025, with 115 Democratic colleagues signed on as cosponsors.

The Speaker referred it to six committees at once — Education and Workforce, House Administration, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary — a split referral that requires multiple committees to act before the bill can reach the floor.
The action record shows nothing after the June 12, 2025 referrals: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion activity appears in the record.
No Republican House member is listed among the bill's 115 cosponsors, and Republicans hold 223 of 440 voting House seats, so the bill's path runs through committees chaired by the opposing party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, household employers and home care companies: none of the bill's new wage, sick time, or contract requirements has taken effect, so they bear no new costs. Domestic workers have gained nothing yet, though the bill remains alive through January 2027.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Household employers and care agencies, for now

sides.party_line_note: All 115 cosponsors are House Democrats; none of the chamber's 223 Republicans has signed on, and no committee action has followed the June 2025 referrals.

industries.industry: Home care and personal care agencies
industries.note: Agencies would face higher labor standards for their aides, but the bill temporarily raises the federal Medicaid match for home care and encourages the use of fiscal intermediaries, routing public money through agency and intermediary structures to fund compliance. That locks the agency role into Medicaid-funded home care while making the workforce more expensive.

The bill bars platforms and employers from docking wages or penalizing workers who communicate directly with customers instead of through the app, and prohibits deductions for breakage or cash shortages — practices built into some platform models.

industries.industry: Private household employers of nannies and housekeepers
industries.note: Wealthier families are the primary direct employers of domestic labor and would bear new wage, sick time, contract, and scheduling costs; middle-income families who hire occasional or part-time help would face much of the same paperwork and cost burden.

The temporary federal match increase for home care delivered by domestic employees would cost the federal government, and states share Medicaid financing; the bill offsets this by delaying enforcement for government-funded programs.
Agencies face the same labor standards for workers they place, but written-contract requirements could push more families toward formal agency arrangements rather than informal cash hires.

analysis.trajectory: With 115 of 217 House Democrats behind it but no Republican cosponsors, a split referral to six committees, and no hearing in the months since introduction, the bill is likely to die in committee as most bills with one-party sponsorship in a divided Congress do. Its realistic paths are narrow: attachment to a larger Democratic package if Democrats retake the House in 2026, or influence at the state level, where a dozen states and cities have already passed domestic worker bills of rights.
